title: An-Naba': the Day of sorting
hookLine: the Day the trumpet sounds and you come in crowds (78:17–18)

cards: A drawer you've been stuffing for years. Receipts, cables, a birthday card, a key to nothing. Everything's in there together, and you can't tell the treasure from the junk anymore.
Then one Saturday you pour it all onto the table and sort it: what matters in one pile, what doesn't in another. Things you'd forgotten turn up.
A life can feel like that drawer: kindnesses and cruelties, the good day and the bad one, all mixed. An-Naba' has asked its question and pointed at the signs.
Now it names the Day itself, and the name it chooses is a sorting word.

teach.b: The verse says: inna yawm al-fasli kana miqata. The Day of fasl is an appointed time. Fasl comes from a root meaning to separate, to divide, to tell one thing from another.
Pickthall translates it as Decision; others say Sorting or Judgment.

teach.h: A CHAPTER, A SEASON, A DAY.
teach.b: In everyday Arabic the same root gives the word for a chapter of a book and for a season of the year: a section cut off from the rest.
So it's the day when what was mixed is separated, and each thing is seen for what it was. Then the picture: the trumpet is blown and you come in crowds, afwaja, wave after wave of people.
The surah describes the garden too, for the ones who were mindful, with gardens and cups and no idle talk.
Then the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks, and no one speaks except whom the Most Merciful permits, and they say what is right.
And it ends with one of the Qur'an's most human lines: on that Day a person will look at what their own hands sent ahead. Every act has already gone on before them, waiting.
And the one who denied it all will say, if only I were dust.

Muslims hold the Day with both hope and fear. The surah isn't naming it to scare anyone into a corner. In its picture, nothing a person did is lost in the drawer; even the smallest kindness gets found.

how: Belief in the Last Day is one of the pillars of faith in Islam; Muslims recite surahs like an-Naba' in prayer and speak of the Day with both hope and fear, often reflecting on their deeds before sleep.

games.q: the Day comes. what does the surah say a person will look at?
o: what their own hands sent ahead
games.why: 78:40: a person will look at what their hands sent ahead. every act has gone on before them.

practice: Think of your days as a long line behind you, and without judging them, let a few rise up: one you're proud of, one you'd rather forget, one ordinary afternoon you'd almost lost.
All of them are yours, and all of them went on ahead. Then turn to today, still being written, and ask what you'd like your hands to send ahead from it; one small thing is enough.

wordCard.voice: An-Naba'. The great news, and the surah that ends by naming the Day of sorting, when each person sees what their hands sent ahead. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Day of sorting, of decision (78:17).

carryVoice: Your line: the day of sorting. Every act goes on ahead. That's day two hundred twenty-one.
